content:
# Make.com (Integromat) Fundamentals ##### The day the linear list stopped being enough Suppose your lead-capture automation needs to do this: take an order, split it into its individual line items, look each one up in inventory, route out-of-stock items to a purchasing workflow and in-stock items to fulfilment, then reassemble everything into one summary email. In a top-to-bottom list of steps, describing that is awkward. You can feel the shape of the logic — it branches, it loops, it rejoins — but the interface wants a straight line. This is where **Make.com** (formerly Integromat) earns its place in your toolkit. Instead of a vertical list, Make gives you a **canvas**: circular modules connected by lines you draw yourself, branching and rejoining visually. Research on visual programming languages (Myers, 1990) argued that spatial layouts help people reason about data flow, and Make is a working demonstration of the claim — complex logic becomes something you can *see*. Today you learn Make's model, rebuild your lead-capture automation on it, and start forming the engineering judgment about which tool fits which job. ##### The canvas, modules, and connections Open a new scenario and you get an empty grid with a single large **+**. Click it and you place your first **module**. A module is one operation — one circle on the canvas, showing the app's logo. Modules come in types you can identify by their icon shape: - **Triggers** (clock or lightning icon) start the scenario. Exactly one, always leftmost. *Instant* triggers are webhooks; *polling* triggers say "Watch..." and check on a schedule. - **Actions** do something: create, update, delete, send. Most modules are these. - **Searches** return zero or more matching records. - **Aggregators, Iterators, Routers** are flow-control modules — tomorrow's territory, but you will see them in the menu. You connect modules by dragging from the small half-circle on a module's right edge to the next module. That line is the **route**, and data flows along it left to right. Unlike Zapier, you *draw* the structure, which is exactly why branches are easy here. ##### Bundles: the concept that unlocks Make This is the single idea that makes Make click, and it is worth slowing down for. In Make, data travels as **bundles**. A bundle is one packet of structured data — think of it as one JSON object, one record, one item. The critical rule: **a module runs once per incoming bundle.** If a module outputs three bundles, every module downstream of it runs three times. A "Watch new rows" module that finds 5 new rows outputs 5 bundles, and the Slack module after it sends 5 messages. That is usually what you want. But it is also why beginners are startled when a scenario suddenly performs 47 operations — some upstream module emitted 47 bundles. Each bundle carries an **operations** cost, which is Make's billing unit: **one module execution on one bundle = one operation**. That differs from Zapier in an important way, which we will come back to. After every run, click any module to open the bubble showing its input and output bundles as an expandable JSON tree: ```json { "Bundle 1": { "id": "2_ABaOnud9c", "created_at": "2026-03-14T09:12:44Z", "answers": { "Full Name": "Ananya Rao", "Email Address": "ananya@example.com", "Company": "Northwind Logistics", "Team Size": "45" } } } ``` Reading these bubbles is Make's equivalent of Zap History, and it is more detailed — you see exactly what went in and what came out of every module, every time. ##### Building and running a scenario Rebuilding your lead-capture automation takes about ten minutes. **1. Place the trigger.** Click **+**, search "Webhooks", choose **Custom webhook**. Click *Add*, name it `lead-capture`, and copy the URL. Now click **Redetermine data structure** — Make goes into listening mode. Send it a sample payload with curl or Postman: ```bash curl -X POST "https://hook.eu2.make.com/g7m2v9qk4dz1x8b6nry3tls0pcw5j" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "name": "Ananya Rao", "email": "ananya@example.com", "company": "Northwind Logistics", "team_size": 45, "message": "Need help automating invoices" }' ``` Make says "Successfully determined." It has now learned the field names — the same "give it real sample data" principle as every other platform. **2. Add an action.** Drag from the trigger's right edge, choose Google Sheets → **Add a Row**. Connect your Google account (OAuth, same as before), pick the spreadsheet and sheet. **3. Map the data.** Click a field and Make opens a panel listing every value available from earlier modules, organized by module. Click `name` and it inserts a token that displays as `1. name` — the `1.` being the module number. You can combine tokens with text and with Make's built-in functions right in the box: `{{upper(1.name)}}` or `{{formatDate(1.created_at; "DD MMM YYYY")}}`. This inline function library is one of Make's real advantages; there is no separate "Formatter step" costing you an operation. **4. Add a second action.** Drag again, add Slack → **Create a Message**, and map a summary line. **5. Run once.** Click **Run once** at the bottom left. Make waits for a webhook, you fire your curl command, and the canvas animates — each module lights up and shows a bubble with its bundle count. Click through them to verify. **6. Schedule and activate.** Toggle the scenario **ON**. ```mermaid flowchart LR W((Webhook
lead-capture)) --> S((Google Sheets
Add a Row)) S --> M((Slack
Create Message)) W -. "1 bundle" .-> S S -. "1 bundle" .-> M ``` ##### Scheduling and the operations pricing model Click the clock icon on the trigger to set scheduling. Options include **Immediately** (webhooks only), **At regular intervals** (every N minutes — as low as 1 minute on paid plans, 15 on free), **Every day** at a set time, **Days of the week/month**, and **Once**. Now the pricing model, because it genuinely changes how you design. **Zapier bills tasks:** roughly one charge per *action step that successfully runs*. Filters, delays and the trigger are free-ish; each action costs. **Make bills operations:** one charge per *module execution per bundle*, including routers, iterators, aggregators and most flow-control modules. The practical consequence: for a **short, simple, low-volume** workflow, Zapier is often cheaper and always simpler. For a **long, high-volume** workflow, Make is usually dramatically cheaper — its plans include far more operations per rupee, and its inline functions mean you do not spend a billable step to uppercase a name. A 10-step workflow running 5,000 times a month would be roughly 50,000 tasks on Zapier (an expensive tier) versus 50,000 operations on Make (a mid-tier plan costing a fraction as much). But watch the bundle multiplication trap: a module that outputs 100 bundles causes every downstream module to run 100 times. A five-module tail on a 100-bundle branch is 500 operations from a single trigger. Filtering early matters even more here than on Zapier. ##### Make vs Zapier: the honest comparison | Dimension | Zapier | Make.com | |---|---|---| | Interface | Vertical list, very simple | Visual canvas, more to learn | | App library | ~7,000+ | ~2,000+ (but strong HTTP module for the rest) | | Branching | Paths (paid, up to ~10) | Routers, unlimited, free-form | | Arrays/loops | Limited Looping step | First-class Iterator/Aggregator | | Transformations | Formatter steps (cost a task) | Inline functions (free within a module) | | Error handling | Basic retries | Per-module error handlers with directives | | Billing | Tasks (actions) | Operations (module × bundle) | | Best for | Non-technical users, quick simple Zaps | Complex logic, arrays, high volume | Neither is "better." Make.com asks for more from you and gives more back. ##### Common pitfalls - **Forgetting to redetermine the data structure** — the mapping panel stays empty and you cannot select fields. - **Not clicking Run once before activating** — you never see whether the mapping was right. - **Ignoring bundle counts** — a scenario quietly performing 300 operations per run will eat a plan in days. - **Confusing the scenario toggle with Run once** — Run once is manual; the toggle makes it live. - **Mapping the wrong module number** — `3. email` and `1. email` can both exist and mean different things. - **Leaving a webhook scenario inactive** — Make queues incoming payloads for a while, then discards them. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task is a direct rebuild: create a free Make.com account and **recreate your lead-capture automation as a scenario** — one trigger module plus at least two action modules, with data mapped between them. Run it once and then *actually open the bundle inspector on each module*. Comparing "what Zapier showed me" with "what Make shows me" for the same automation is the fastest way to understand both. For the mini project, go a step further: a scenario that watches for a new email (or webhook), extracts key fields, adds a Google Sheets row, and posts a summary to Slack or Discord — then **schedule it** to run automatically rather than manually. The assignment asks you to write the **Zapier vs Make comparison** covering interface, pricing model (tasks vs operations) and flexibility, and to pick one for a 10-step, high-volume workflow. Argue it with numbers: estimate monthly runs, multiply by steps, and price both. That quantified reasoning is exactly what a client or employer wants to see. ##### Key takeaways - Make.com replaces the linear list with a canvas of modules and hand-drawn routes, which makes branching and rejoining logic visible. - Data moves as bundles, and a module runs once per incoming bundle — bundle counts drive both behaviour and cost. - Build rhythm: place trigger → redetermine data structure with real sample data → add modules → map with inline functions → Run once → activate. - Zapier bills per action (task); Make bills per module execution per bundle (operation). Long, high-volume scenarios are usually far cheaper on Make. - Choose Zapier for speed and simplicity, Make for complex logic, arrays, and scale — and be able to justify the choice with an estimate.
